power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.052", "p = 0.052"), Sentence = c("147 For walking time to the nearest health facility, 31-60 minutes (aPR: 1.60, 95% CI: 1.08-2.36) 148 and 1-2 hours or longer (aPR: 1.56, 95% CI: 1.05-2.33) were associated with higher prevalence 149 than less than 15 minutes, although the overall association with walking time was not statistically 150 significant (p = 0.052).", "The overall association with walking time to the nearest health facility was not statistically significant (p = 0.052), although category-specific estimates were higher for longer walking times." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Background: Children who have not received the first dose of a diphtheria-tetanus-pertussiscontaining vaccine are classified as zero-dose.
Understanding how many children remain without this dose beyond infancy, the correlates, and their geographic distribution can inform routine and catch-up vaccination services in Ethiopia.
This study aimed to estimate the burden of zero-dose, identify its correlates, and map its spatial distribution among children aged 12-35 months in Ethiopia.

Methods: We analyzed data from 2,097 children aged 12-35 months in the Pathways for Ethiopia survey, a recent national population-based cross-sectional household survey conducted from August to November 2025.
The burden estimates and regression analyses accounted for sampling weights, stratification, and clustering.
Adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) were obtained through marginal standardization of survey-weighted logistic regression models.
Spatial autocorrelation, hotspot, and spatial-scan analyses assessed geographic clustering.
Ordinary kriging predicted prevalence at unsampled locations.
The weighted prevalence of zero-dose status was 20.6% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 15.9-26.3), with regional point estimates ranging from 0.8% in Addis Ababa to 35.9% in Somali.
Its burden was 20.4% among children aged 12-23 months and 20.8% among those aged 24-35 months.

Higher burden was associated with no antenatal care compared with four or more visits (aPR: 2.39; 95% CI: 1.61-3.53), unimproved compared with improved drinking-water sources (aPR: 1.52; 95% CI: 1.18-1.97), and caregivers rating vaccination as less than very important compared with very important (aPR: 2.68; 95% CI: 2.03-3.54).
Zero-dose prevalence showed significant spatial clustering (Moran's I = 0.229; p = 0.0001).
Hotspots occurred among sampled communities in Somali, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, Afar, and South Ethiopia.
Predicted prevalence was highest across parts of eastern and south-central Ethiopia.
Conclusion: Approximately one in five children aged 12-35 months had not received the first pentavalent dose.
High zero-dose prevalence clustered among sampled communities in eastern and south-central Ethiopia.
Moreover, antenatal care and drinking water source were independent factors.
Immunization programs should prioritize these communities for identifying and vaccinating missed children, including those aged 24-35 months.
Childhood immunization prevents serious illness and death, yet millions of children continue to miss essential vaccine doses.
Children who have not received the first dose of a diphtheriatetanus-pertussis-containing vaccine (DTP1) are classified as zero-dose [1].

text.text: These studies establish the importance of geographic and population differences, while leaving a need for updated national evidence that includes older children who remain without a first dose.
As catch-up services expand, understanding the size and geographic distribution of this unmet vaccination need can help determine whom to reach and where to focus vaccination activities.

Using a national population-based household survey conducted in 2025, this study aimed to estimate national and regional zero-dose prevalence among children aged 12-35 months in Ethiopia, identify correlates among child, maternal, household, and service characteristics, and examine spatial clustering and geographic patterns of zero-dose status.

This study used data from the Pathways for Ethiopia national population-based cross-sectional household survey, conducted from August to November 2025 across all 12 regional states and the two chartered cities.
Information on children was collected in the survey of women of reproductive age.
The survey used a stratified two-stage cluster sampling design.
In the first stage, census enumeration areas (EAs) were stratified by region and urban-rural residence and selected for the survey.
In the second stage, eligible women were listed and sampled within the selected EAs.
Fieldwork was completed in 247 of the 251 planned EAs.
The analysis included children aged 12-35 months whose first pentavalent dose status could be determined from the survey.
Records with incomplete or invalid sampling or geographic information were excluded.
Zero-dose status was defined as nonreceipt of the first pentavalent dose, a diphtheria-tetanuspertussis-containing vaccine.
Vaccination status was assessed from vaccination records and caregiver reports, with records taking precedence when available.

The independent variables were child age, region, residence, maternal age, maternal education, household financial situation, water and sanitation, antenatal care (ANC), place of delivery, walking time to the nearest health facility, self-reported local armed conflict, participation in decisions about child healthcare, and perceived vaccination importance.
Caregivers rated the importance of vaccines for their child's health on a four-point scale: "not at all important," "a little important," "moderately important," or "very important" [7].

Predictions were generated on a 10-km grid using the 16 nearest EAs.
The exponential model was further evaluated using five geographically separated validation groups.
Its prediction error was compared with that of a prediction based on the pooled prevalence in the training sample.
Geographic variation in associations with zero-dose status was examined using binomial models with a spatial intercept and a spatially varying coefficient.
Ten contrasts involving child, maternal, household and service characteristics were assessed among children with complete model data.
Tests of geographic variation were adjusted for multiple comparisons, and spatial cross-validation compared each model with a corresponding constant-coefficient model.
Local odds ratios were mapped for contrasts showing geographic variation and improved prediction, at locations with sufficient observations in both comparison groups.
Each odds ratio compared the specified category with its reference group.
The study included 2,097 children aged 12-35 months in 247 sampled EAs, of whom 311 were zero-dose.

text.text: For one to three compared with at least four ANC visits (q = 0.015), local odds ratios ranged from 0.23 to 2.09 across 105 communities with adequate local data, with higher values in some central sampled communities.

Both spatially varying models performed slightly better than the constant-coefficient models in spatial cross-validation.
Approximately one in five children aged 12-35 months had not received the first pentavalent dose in 2025.
Zero-dose status was associated with maternal healthcare use, household living conditions and perceptions of vaccination.
High zero-dose prevalence clustered in sampled communities in eastern and south-central Ethiopia.
These findings show that missed first doses remain a substantial concern beyond infancy and identify communities where vaccination services should be strengthened.

The 20.6% prevalence (95% CI: 15.9-26.3) was broadly comparable to the 23.7% reported by Muchie and colleagues from the 2019 Mini Demographic and Health Survey of children aged 12-23 months [3] and the 24.8% reported by Endehabtu and colleagues from a 2023 programme evaluation of the same younger age group in ten regions and two cities [4].

text.text: The repeated identification of high-prevalence areas supports prioritizing these communities when planning outreach and identifying children who have missed vaccination.
ANC was found to be a factor associated with zero-dose among children.
Children whose mothers reported no ANC visits had higher zero-dose prevalence as compared with those mothers reported four or more visits.
This finding is consistent with the study conducted in Kenya [24] and Ethiopia in 2019 [3].
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with the study conducted in Kenya <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[24]</ref> and Ethiopia in 2019 <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[3]</ref>.

text.text: The observed association between ANC attendance and childhood vaccination may also reflect broader engagement with the healthcare system, as mothers who attend ANC may be more likely to use immunization services for their children.
ANC visits may provide opportunities for mothers to receive information about childhood vaccination schedules and develop trust in vaccination services [4].
text.formatted: ANC visits may provide opportunities for mothers to receive information about childhood vaccination schedules and develop trust in vaccination services <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Lower perceived vaccination importance was also strongly associated with zero-dose status.
Endehabtu and colleagues similarly reported an association involving caregivers' perceptions of vaccination benefits [4].

text.text: Reviews of childhood immunization have identified parental attitudes, limited information and communication barriers among the reasons for non-vaccination [26, 27].

text.text: These findings support clear explanations of vaccination benefits and opportunities for caregivers to discuss their concerns.
Because perceptions and vaccination status were measured at the same time, present views may precede missed vaccination or reflect previous service encounters.
An unimproved drinking-water source was noted as a factor associated with zero-dose status.
Children living in households with unimproved drinking water sources had 52% higher prevalence of zero-dose as compared with those living in households with improved drinking water sources.
Water source may reflect household living conditions and access to basic services.

Wendt and colleagues, using surveys from 80 low-and middle-income countries, found that children who had received no DTP-containing vaccine were more likely to experience other forms of deprivation, with particularly consistent associations involving water, sanitation and maternal education [28].

text.text: An analysis across 33 sub-Saharan African countries also linked receipt of no vaccine with household wealth and maternal healthcare use [29].
text.formatted: An analysis across 33 sub-Saharan African countries also linked receipt of no vaccine with household wealth and maternal healthcare use <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[29]</ref>.

text.text: Limited access to improved water and vaccination may therefore reflect overlapping household disadvantages.
The finding supports considering broader living conditions when identifying children missed by immunization services.
In the descriptive analysis, zero-dose prevalence was higher among rural children and those whose mothers reported non-institutional delivery.
However, the adjusted prevalence ratios did not show statistically significant associations with either residence or place of delivery.
In the 2019 Mini Demographic and Health Survey, Muchie and colleagues did report adjusted associations with rural residence and noninstitutional delivery [3].

text.text: Maternal education, household financial situation and sanitation also showed no clear overall adjusted association in the present study.
Earlier Ethiopian research on full vaccination found inequalities by wealth and maternal education [16].
text.formatted: Earlier Ethiopian research on full vaccination found inequalities by wealth and maternal education <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[16]</ref>.

text.text: Differences in vaccination outcomes, populations and covariate adjustment may contribute to these findings.
Full vaccination measures completion of several doses, so those findings do not directly contradict results for first-dose nonreceipt.
The absence of a clear adjusted association here does not establish that these characteristics are unrelated to vaccination access.
The overall association with walking time to the nearest health facility was not statistically significant (p = 0.052), although category-specific estimates were higher for longer walking times.
Okwaraji and colleagues found lower third-pentavalent-dose coverage among children living at least an hour from a health post in rural northwestern Ethiopia [30].
text.formatted: Okwaraji and colleagues found lower third-pentavalent-dose coverage among children living at least an hour from a health post in rural northwestern Ethiopia <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Their study included children aged 12-59 months and used geographically estimated travel time, whereas the present survey used reported walking time and examined first-dose nonreceipt.
The present estimates suggest a possible access barrier, although the overall association was not statistically conclusive.

Self-reported local armed conflict was associated with lower zero-dose prevalence (aPR: 0.70, 95% CI: 0.50-0.99), and children whose mothers decided alone on child healthcare had lower prevalence than those with joint decisions (aPR: 0.64, 95% CI: 0.44-0.94).
The timing and intensity of reported conflict in relation to vaccination were not established.
Household decisionmaking responses did not identify who arranged or provided vaccination.
Qualitative research in underserved Ethiopian communities identified gender norms and limited support for caregivers as barriers to childhood vaccination [25].
text.formatted: Qualitative research in underserved Ethiopian communities identified gender norms and limited support for caregivers as barriers to childhood vaccination <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[25]</ref>.

text.text: The decision-making association may therefore reflect household circumstances not fully captured by the response categories.
Both inverse associations may be affected by residual confounding and should not be interpreted as protective effects.
The associations of ANC attendance and participation in decisions about child healthcare with zero-dose status varied across sampled communities with adequate local data.
Endehabtu and colleagues also reported geographic variation in associations involving ANC and vaccination perceptions [4].

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that national average associations may not describe every locality.
The local maps can help guide assessment of maternal healthcare use and household decision-making in the identified communities.
The local analyses identified concentrations of high zero-dose prevalence within the broader regional pattern.
Four communities were classified as high-high clusters and nine as hotspots in Somali; the primary scan cluster extended across parts of Somali, Oromia and Sidama.
Nigerian surveys have also mapped zero-dose concentrations while examining first-dose status separately from other vaccination outcomes [31, 32].

text.text: Although their city sample differs from a national survey, the findings illustrate how local concentrations can cross administrative borders.
Coordination between neighbouring service areas may therefore help reach children in the identified clusters.
The predicted surface showed higher prevalence in parts of eastern and south-central Ethiopia, consistent with the clusters identified in sampled communities.
Spatial cross-validation showed a modest reduction in prediction error compared with predictions based on the pooled prevalence in the training sample.

The 2024-25 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey reported first-pentavalent-dose receipt in 70.6% of children aged 12-23 months, equivalent to 29.4% without the dose, based on vaccination cards or maternal reports [41].
The present study found first-dose nonreceipt of 20.6% among children aged 12-35 months.
Differences in age eligibility and survey methods limit direct comparison.
Nevertheless, both surveys indicate a substantial unmet need for firstdose vaccination beyond infancy.
The mapped concentrations support prioritizing first-dose vaccination services in the identified communities.
The primary scan zone crossed Somali, Oromia and Sidama, suggesting that reaching missed children may require coordination across neighbouring service areas.
Reliable outreach and clear information for caregivers are relevant priorities, consistent with barriers reported in underserved Ethiopian settings [25].

text.text: Identifying zero-dose children should therefore be accompanied by follow-up to complete the recommended doses.

This study drew on a national survey covering Ethiopia's regional states and chartered cities, accounted for complex sampling in prevalence estimates and adjusted association analyses, and examined geographic clustering using several spatial methods.

This study finding might present with limitations such as a reporting bias as zero-dose status was assessed from vaccination records and caregiver reports; incomplete records and recall errors may affect classification.
Several regional estimates were imprecise and some EAs included few eligible children.
Maternal health-service information referred to the woman's most recent eligible pregnancy and may not relate to the pregnancy of the child included in this analysis.
The predicted values depend on the distribution of sampled EAs, which limits local interpretation, as discussed in other spatial vaccination studies.
The cross-sectional design and correlated household and service factors preclude causal attribution.
Approximately one in five children aged 12-35 months had not received the first pentavalent dose.
ANC utilization, drinking-water sources, and caregivers' perceived importance of vaccination were associated with higher zero-dose prevalence.
High prevalence clustered among sampled communities in eastern and south-central Ethiopia.
Immunization programmes should prioritize identifying and vaccinating missed children in these communities, including those aged 24-35 months, through age-appropriate catch-up services.
Strengthening links between maternal healthcare and immunization, addressing caregiver concerns, and reviewing the regularity and reach of outreach services are relevant programme priorities.
Local planning should combine the geographic findings with current service and household information.
